title: The Subura to the Curia of Pompey: nine years in Gaul, the river crossed, and twenty-three wounds
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Subura House and the Marian Inheritance

stops.name: Rome, the Subura: a patrician born into Marius's family
stops.date_confidence: Year attested by standard modern chronology, though some older reconstructions argued 102 BC. Day traditional, 12 or 13 July. Place reconstruction: Suetonius's opening chapters are lost and no ancient text names the house or the district. The Subura association most plausibly reflects his later residence there, attested until his election as pontifex maximus in 63 BC, rather than his birthplace. Coordinate placed on the Quirinal-Viminal slope, Via Urbana area, not the Imperial Fora zone west of it.
stops.campa: In the crowded quarter between the Quirinal and the Viminal that Romans call the Subura, a son is born to Gaius Julius Caesar the praetor and his wife Aurelia. The chapters of Suetonius that would have named the day and the house do not survive, and the quarter itself is an inference from where he is attested living forty years later. The family is patrician and old, and it has had no consul in living memory. It claims descent from the goddess Venus through Aeneas and his son Iulus. It has also just married into the party of Gaius Marius, who is the boy's uncle by marriage.
suggested_refs: The Subura quarter on the Quirinal-Viminal slopes, progressively built over by the Forum of Caesar, the Forum of Augustus and Trajan's Forum

stops.name: Pisae: the father dead putting on his shoes
stops.date_confidence: Year per standard chronology placing the death in Caesar's sixteenth year; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01. Pliny reports the manner of death but not the date. Coordinate is the settled site of ancient Pisae.
stops.campa: Caesar's father, who has been praetor and then governor of Asia, dies suddenly one morning at Pisae while putting on his shoes. Pliny sets the death down in a catalogue of men who died without warning, a bare entry among natural curiosities. The son is sixteen. He inherits a patrician name, a marriage connection to the Marian party, no consulship in the family for generations, and the headship of a household in a city where Marius and Sulla are preparing to settle their quarrel by proscription lists.
sources: Pliny, Natural History 7.181 (reported in dossier, not fetched)
suggested_refs: Pliny's catalogue of sudden deaths, Natural History book 7

stops.name: Rome, the Capitol: priest of Jupiter, husband of Cinna's daughter
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction inside the research pool, flagged and not resolved. The chronology lens gave 87 BC and the geography lens 87/86 BC, both of which precede the father's death in 85. Suetonius, Divus Julius 1: 'In the course of his sixteenth year he lost his father. In the next consulate, having previously been nominated priest of Jupiter, he broke his engagement with Cossutia... and married Cornelia.' The next consulate after 85 is 84. Some scholars allow 86/85. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01. Whether he was ever fully inaugurated as flamen, as against merely nominated, is disputed.
stops.campa: In the consulate after his father's death, under the Cinnan regime, the young man is nominated flamen Dialis, priest of Jupiter on the Capitol. In the same stroke of policy he breaks his engagement to the wealthy Cossutia and marries Cornelia, daughter of Cinna, four times consul. Priesthood and marriage are arranged by the same people in the same season, and the sources do not agree on whether the inauguration is ever completed. The office he is nominated to is a cage of taboos: no horse, no army under arms, no night spent outside the city, no knot anywhere on the body, not in the belt and not in the hair.
suggested_refs: The Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus on the Capitol, seat of the flaminate
Modern scholarship on whether Caesar was inaugurated flamen Dialis or only nominated

stops.name: The Sabine hills: a night's lodging at a time
stops.date_confidence: Attested that the flight happened; Plutarch places it in Sabine territory. No source preserves the village, the house, or the duration, so the coordinate is an approximate regional centroid and not a landmark. Date is the year of Sulla's victory; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Sulla, master of Italy, orders the young man to divorce Cinna's daughter. Others have divorced at command. Caesar refuses, and loses the priesthood, Cornelia's dowry and his inheritance in a single stroke. He goes into the Sabine hill country and moves lodging every night, sick with a quartan fever, one name away from the proscription lists. Relatives and the Vestal Virgins petition Sulla until he gives way, remarking, so the story runs, that in this young man there are many Mariuses. No source preserves the village or the house.
sources: Plutarch, Life of Caesar 1 (Penelope/Loeb, fetched): 'he hid himself for some time, wandering about in the country of the Sabines'
suggested_refs: The Sullan proscription lists of 82-81 BC

segments.name: Asia, the Crown of Oak, and the Pirates

stops.name: Mytilene: a wreath of oak leaves for a life saved
stops.date_confidence: Corrected from the pool's internal disagreement: the chronology lens gave 80 BC, the geography lens gave 81/80. Wikipedia, 'Mytilene' dates the siege to 81 BC and both are harmonized to 81 here. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Serving on the staff of Marcus Minucius Thermus in Asia, Caesar goes over the wall at the storming of Mytilene and brings a Roman soldier out alive. Thermus awards him the corona civica, a wreath of oak leaves given for saving the life of a citizen in battle. It is the highest thing the army has short of the crown for first over a wall, and it carries a privilege: when a man wearing it enters the theatre, the audience stands, senators included. This is how Rome first hears his name. He is nineteen.
sources: Suetonius, Divus Julius 2 (Penelope/Loeb, fetched): 'at the storming of Mytilene Thermus awarded him the civic crown'
suggested_refs: The corona civica and its privileges in Roman military honours

stops.name: Nicomedia: the errand at the Bithynian court
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Caesar was sent to Nicomedes IV to fetch ships and that he returned a second time. The sexual allegation is reconstruction and tradition, unprovable in either direction; Suetonius reports it as suspicion, not as fact. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Sent to King Nicomedes of Bithynia to fetch a fleet, Caesar stays at the court longer than the errand needs, and goes back a second time on a freedman's business. Suetonius records the visit under suspicion of improper relations with the king. The story sticks for forty years. Soldiers sing it in the ranks at his own Gallic triumph and it is thrown at him in the Senate; he denies it under oath, and the denial changes nothing. In his edicts as consul, Bibulus calls him 'the queen of Bithynia'.
suggested_refs: Bibulus's edicts of 59 BC and the soldiers' songs at the Gallic triumph, both preserved in Suetonius

stops.name: Rome, the Forum: two governors prosecuted, two cases lost
stops.date_confidence: Two prosecutions in two years, which the chronology lens had collapsed onto one date. Gnaeus Cornelius Dolabella, 77 BC; Gaius Antonius Hybrida, 76 BC. The stop is dated to the first. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01. Source is the Suetonius and Cicero tradition, not independently re-fetched this pass. No ancient source specifies where in the Forum the courts sat, so the general Forum coordinate is used.
stops.campa: Back in Rome under the restored Sullan order, Caesar prosecutes Gnaeus Cornelius Dolabella, consular and former governor of Macedonia, for extortion in his province. Dolabella is defended by the two best advocates in the city and acquitted. The following year Caesar tries again, against Gaius Antonius Hybrida, and loses again. He wins nothing at law. He has stood up in the Forum twice, in public, a patrician in his twenties against the men Sulla left in place. The speeches are published and they circulate.
sources: Dossier, citing the Suetonius and Cicero tradition on Caesar's early oratory; not independently re-verified this session
suggested_refs: Cicero's Brutus on Caesar's oratory
The published texts of the Dolabella prosecution, lost

stops.name: Pharmacusa: forty days, and the promise they took for a joke
stops.date_confidence: Attested capture; the length of captivity is a live discrepancy, retained: Suetonius gives nearly forty days, Plutarch thirty-eight. Year is the conventional dating; month and day unknown, defaulted to 02-01 to order the segment. The tradition that he fitted out the pursuit fleet at Miletus is reconstruction and is not in the Suetonius or Plutarch text fetched.
stops.campa: Sailing east to study rhetoric, Caesar is taken by Cilician pirates off the little island of Pharmacusa and held while the ransom is raised. Twenty talents, they say. He tells them the figure is an insult and orders them to demand fifty. He writes verses and speeches in captivity and reads them aloud to his captors, calling them illiterate barbarians when they fail to admire, and promises them, in what they take for a joke, that he will come back and crucify them. Thirty-eight days, says Plutarch; forty, says Suetonius. Ransomed, he raises ships at once, takes them at their anchorage, and crucifies them.
sources: Unconfirmed strand of the wider tradition placing the fitting-out of the pursuit fleet at Miletus
suggested_refs: The island of Farmakonisi in the Dodecanese
Caesar's earlier service under Publius Servilius Vatia against the Cilician pirates, standard ancient tradition, not independently verified

stops.name: Rhodes: the school of Apollonius Molon
stops.date_confidence: Attested study at Rhodes under Apollonius Molon. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 09-01 to order the segment after the captivity. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from cicero.journey.json, which carries its own Rhodes stop for the same teacher a few years earlier.
stops.campa: He goes on to Rhodes and enrolls with Apollonius Molon, the rhetorician whose school Cicero had left a few years earlier with his voice and his lungs remade. Plutarch says Caesar had as much natural talent for political oratory as anyone of his generation and worked at it until he held an undisputed second rank, declining to press for first because he intended to be first at something else. The lessons are interrupted when Mithridates moves: Caesar crosses to Asia without authority, raises troops on his own credit, and drives the king's officer out of the province.
sources: cicero.journey.json, stop 'Rhodes, Apollonius Molon and the tears of the Greek master'
suggested_refs: The rhetorical school of Apollonius Molon at Rhodes, where Cicero had studied in 79-77 BC

stops.name: Gades: weeping at the statue of Alexander
stops.date_confidence: Attested episode, reported by both Suetonius and Plutarch, though the two differ on whether the statue or a reading of Alexander's deeds prompted the tears. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 03-01 to order the segment. The exact site of the Temple of Hercules Gaditanus within ancient Gades is not fixed by the sources fetched, so city-centre coordinates are used as an approximation.
stops.campa: Quaestor in Further Spain, going the circuit of the assize courts, Caesar comes to Gades and to the temple of Hercules, where a statue of Alexander stands. He reads, he works out the arithmetic, and he weeps: Alexander at this same age had already conquered the world, and Caesar has done nothing anyone would write down. That night, the story runs, he dreams of violating his own mother, and the soothsayers tell him the mother is the earth and the dream promises him rule over her. He asks to be released from the province and goes home early.
stops.quote: it is matter for sorrow that while Alexander, at my age, was already king of so many peoples, I have as yet achieved no brilliant success
stops.quote_source: Plutarch, Life of Caesar 11 (Loeb translation, LacusCurtius)
suggested_refs: The Temple of Hercules Gaditanus at Gades and its Alexander statue
alexander.journey.json

stops.name: Rome, the Rostra: the images of Marius carried out again
stops.date_confidence: Attested, transmitted through Suetonius, Divus Julius 6, which preserves the genealogy speech. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 07-01. The two orations, for his aunt Julia and for his wife Cornelia, fall in the same year and are treated as one scene.
stops.campa: From the Rostra, Caesar speaks the funeral oration for his aunt Julia, widow of Gaius Marius. He traces her descent, and his own, from the kings of Rome on the mother's side and from the immortal gods on the father's, and then does the thing nobody has dared since Sulla died: he has the images of Marius carried in the procession, in daylight, in the Forum. Old soldiers weep and the Sullan party protests to no effect. In the same year he buries Cornelia and speaks over her too, which is not the custom for a young wife.
suggested_refs: The Rostra in the Forum Romanum
The funeral imagines of Gaius Marius, banned from public display under the Sullan settlement

stops.name: Rome, the Capitol: the aedile's games and the trophies restored
stops.date_confidence: Attested, Suetonius, Divus Julius 10. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01, the start of the aedilician year. The specific figure for the resulting debt is not in the verified pool and is not stated.
stops.campa: As curule aedile alongside Marcus Bibulus he decorates the Forum, the Comitium and the Capitol, throws up temporary colonnades to show his collections, and puts on gladiatorial games on a scale that frightens the Senate into capping how many fighters a private man may keep in the city. Overnight, without asking, he has the trophies of Marius restored to the Capitol, gilded, so that Rome finds them there at dawn. Bibulus complains that a joint aedileship is remembered as Caesar's alone. None of it is paid for out of money he has, and no source gives the size of what he owes at the end of the year.
sources: Suetonius, Divus Julius 10 (Penelope/Loeb, fetched): 'decorated the Forum, Comitium, and Capitol... gave gladiatorial shows'
suggested_refs: The senatorial decree limiting privately owned gladiators at Rome, passed in response to Caesar's games

stops.name: Rome, the Domus Publica: pontifex maximus
stops.date_confidence: Attested election, Suetonius, Divus Julius 13. The day is the conventional dating of the pontifical election of 63 BC and is used to order the segment before the December Catilinarian debate. Caesar's co-option into the college of pontiffs in 73 BC has no separate stop and is folded into this scene.
stops.campa: The chief priesthood of the Roman state falls vacant and Caesar stands for it against Quintus Lutatius Catulus and Publius Servilius Isauricus, both former consuls, both far senior, both certain of it. Catulus offers him money to stand down. He borrows more instead and spends it on the tribes, until the debt is past the point where losing is survivable. On the morning of the vote he tells his mother at the door that he will come back pontifex maximus or not come back. He wins, and carries his opponents' own tribes. The office is held for life and it comes with a house on the Sacred Way.
sources: Suetonius, Divus Julius 13 (Penelope/Loeb, fetched): 'he would never return except as pontifex'
suggested_refs: The Domus Publica beside the Regia, official residence of the pontifex maximus
Caesar's co-option into the college of pontiffs, 73 BC

stops.name: Rome, the Temple of Concord: the argument against the executions
stops.date_confidence: Attested session and date. The place name is corrected: the pool labelled this the Curia, but the 5 December session met in the Temple of Concord, where Cicero delivered the Fourth Catilinarian. The pool's coordinate is right for Concord and is kept; the Curia Julia lies about 120 m east. Caesar's speech itself survives only as Sallust's literary reconstruction, Bellum Catilinae 51, not as a transcript.
stops.campa: The Catilinarian conspirators are under arrest and the Senate meets in the Temple of Concord to decide what to do with them. Caesar, praetor-elect, argues that Roman citizens may not be put to death without trial: confiscate the property, distribute the men among the towns of Italy, hold them in perpetual confinement, and above all set no precedent that a later faction will use on somebody else. The consul Cicero wavers toward him. Cato answers for execution and carries the house. On the way out, young men of the guard draw swords on Caesar, and he stays away from the Senate for the rest of the year.
sources: Sallust, Bellum Catilinae 51 (literary reconstruction of the speech, not a transcript)
Wikipedia, 'Catiline Orations' (fetched): the Fourth Catilinarian delivered in the Temple of Concord, 5 December 63 BC
suggested_refs: The Temple of Concord at the western end of the Forum Romanum
cicero.journey.json

stops.name: Rome, the Domus Publica: the Bona Dea and the divorce
stops.date_confidence: Well attested in the ancient tradition through Plutarch and Cicero, though the specific chapters were not re-fetched this pass. The rites fall in early December; the exact night is not fixed, and 12-04 is used to order the segment. Caesar's praetorship of 62 and his brief suspension from office over Metellus Nepos belong to the same year and have no separate stop.
stops.campa: The rites of the Bona Dea are held each December in the house of the pontifex maximus: women only, the men of the household turned out for the night, Caesar's mother and his sister presiding. Publius Clodius Pulcher comes in dressed as a woman and is found out. At the trial that follows, Caesar is called as a witness and swears he knows nothing against anybody, which acquits Clodius. He has nonetheless divorced Pompeia already, and when the court asks him to reconcile the two things, he does not say that anything happened.
stops.quote: Because Caesar's wife must be free from suspicion.
stops.quote_source: Plutarch, Moralia, Sayings of Romans (Caesar, no. 3), LacusCurtius. The commoner English phrasing 'above suspicion' is a later paraphrase, not this translation.
sources: Dossier synthesis of the Plutarch and Suetonius tradition on the Bona Dea affair, not independently re-fetched this session
Suetonius, Divus Julius 13 for the office and residence
suggested_refs: The trial of Publius Clodius Pulcher, 61 BC
Caesar's praetorship of 62 BC and his suspension over the proposals of Metellus Nepos

stops.name: Brigantium: the road west ends at the ocean
stops.date_confidence: Attested campaign, attested acclamation as imperator. The identification of the Atlantic terminus with Brigantium, modern A Coruna, is a standard modern reconstruction: no ancient text fetched names the exact site. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 06-01 to order the segment.
stops.campa: Propraetor of Further Spain, Caesar raises ten new cohorts on his own initiative and marches against the Lusitanian and Callaecan hill communities, driving west until the road runs out at the ocean. Ships come up the coast behind him and the islanders are made to submit. He settles the province's debt disputes in a way that satisfies neither creditors nor debtors entirely, takes enough plunder to clear his own creditors and still send money to the treasury, and is hailed imperator by the army in the field. No ancient text names the point on the Atlantic where he stopped.
stops.quote: I would rather be first here than second at Rome
stops.quote_source: Plutarch, Life of Caesar 11 (Loeb translation, LacusCurtius), reported as said while passing a wretched village in the Alps on the road to Spain
sources: Wikipedia chronology, 'Governs Further Spain; hailed imperator'
suggested_refs: The Roman Brigantium at A Coruna, conventional identification of the Atlantic terminus

stops.name: Rome: the consulship, and three men who agree in private
stops.date_confidence: Attested consulship, dated to the calendar year. The private alliance of Caesar, Pompey and Crassus is formed in 60 BC and is standard reconstruction from Cicero, Suetonius, Plutarch and Appian; the label 'First Triumvirate' is modern and was never a Roman institution.
stops.campa: Caesar comes home to find that a triumph and a consulship cannot be had in the same season, and gives up the triumph. Then he does the thing that changes the shape of the Republic: he reconciles Pompey and Crassus, who have loathed each other for ten years, and binds the three of them privately to let nothing be done in the state that any one of them dislikes. As consul he carries the land law over his colleague Bibulus, who retires to his house and announces he is watching the sky for unfavourable omens. Caesar takes Gaul and Illyricum for five years.
sources: Suetonius, Divus Julius (Penelope/Loeb): 'Held with Marcus Bibulus... passed agrarian laws and dominated state affairs'
Wikipedia chronology; standard reconstruction from Cicero, Suetonius, Plutarch, Appian
suggested_refs: The lex Vatinia and the senatorial addition of Transalpine Gaul to Caesar's command

stops.name: Geneva: the bridge over the Rhone broken
stops.date_confidence: Attested from Caesar's own Bellum Gallicum book 1. Wikipedia, 'Geneva' confirms Caesar's own use of the name Genava. The Helvetian migration is dated to spring 58 BC; the day is not fixed and 04-01 is used to order the segment.
stops.campa: Word comes that the Helvetii have burned their own towns, twelve of them and four hundred villages, and are moving west with an entire nation and its carts. Caesar covers the road from Rome to Geneva in eight days, breaks the bridge over the Rhone, and puts up nineteen miles of rampart and ditch along the river to close the easy way. When their envoys ask for passage he uses the time the wall has bought and refuses them. Then he crosses the Alps with five legions and goes after them.
stops.quote: All Gaul is divided into three parts, one of which the Belgae inhabit, the Aquitani another, those who in their own language are called Celts, in our Gauls, the third.
stops.quote_source: Caesar, Commentarii de Bello Gallico 1.1, translated W. A. McDevitte and W. S. Bohn (1869), Perseus Digital Library. The opening sentence of the work whose events begin here.
suggested_refs: The Rhone bridge at Genava and the nineteen-mile line of rampart

stops.name: Bibracte: the horses sent away
stops.date_confidence: Attested battle. The name is traditional: Wikipedia, 'Bibracte' places the actual fighting about 26 km south of the oppidum, near Montmort, so the coordinate marks the associated site and not the battlefield. Month and day approximate, 07-01. The defeat of Ariovistus near the Rhine in September of the same year is attested as an event but no source fetched fixes a battlefield; it has no separate stop and is folded into this scene.
stops.campa: Caesar shadows the migration for a fortnight, cuts up the Tigurini at the crossing of the Arar, then turns aside toward Bibracte for grain and is attacked on the march. He sends the horses to the rear, his own first, so that no man in the line can outrun another. The legions fight uphill against a moving nation for most of a day and into the night. The survivors are sent home and ordered to rebuild the towns they burned. That autumn Gallic chiefs ask him to deal with Ariovistus, a German king the Senate has formally called a friend of Rome, and he breaks him near the Rhine and drives the remnant across the water.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Bibracte' (fetched): battle fought near Montmort, 26 km south of the oppidum
suggested_refs: The Mont Beuvray oppidum of the Aedui
The unresolved battlefield of the Ariovistus campaign in Alsace

stops.name: The river Sabis: a shield taken from a man in the rear rank
stops.date_confidence: The battle is well attested from Caesar's own book 2; the site is a reconstruction. Coordinate follows Wikipedia, 'Battle of the Sabis' and Turquin (1955), placing it on the west bank of the Selle near Saulzoir. The older identification with the Sambre near Aulnoye-Aymeries is still live scholarship. Month and day approximate, 07-01. The pool's earlier coordinate, 16 km SSE near Le Cateau-Cambresis, is superseded.
stops.campa: The Nervii, who let no wine and no merchants into their country in case their people go soft, are waiting in the woods across the river while the legions are still marking out a camp. They come down so fast that men fight without helmets and without finding their own standards, and two legions are surrounded on the left. Caesar takes a shield off a soldier in the rear rank, goes into the front line himself, and calls the centurions by name. The Nervii die where they stand. Of sixty thousand fighting men, Caesar writes, five hundred were left, and of six hundred senators, three.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Battle of the Sabis' (fetched), coordinates and the Turquin identification
suggested_refs: The Selle near Saulzoir, and the competing Sambre identification of the ancient Sabis

stops.name: Aduatuca: fifty-three thousand sold to the traders
stops.date_confidence: The episode and the figure are attested from Caesar's own account, which is to say they are his own numbers in a work written to be read at Rome. The Namur-area identification of the Aduatuci stronghold is the standard modern placement and was not independently re-verified this pass. Month and day approximate, 09-01.
stops.campa: The Aduatuci shut themselves into their one strong town and stand on the wall watching the Romans assemble a siege tower a mile off, laughing at the size of the men who mean to push it. When it starts to move they surrender, and throw their weapons over the wall into the ditch, keeping back a third of them. That night they come out and are cut down against the entrenchments. In the morning Caesar opens the town and sells the population to the traders who follow the army. He gives the number himself, in his own dispatch to Rome: fifty-three thousand persons.
sources: Dossier; the Namur-area site identification is standard modern scholarship, not re-verified this pass
suggested_refs: The slave traders attached to Roman armies in Gaul, and the market that absorbed the Aduatuci

stops.name: Quiberon Bay: the halyards cut with hooks
stops.date_confidence: Attested engagement. Coordinate corrected to Wikipedia, 'Battle of Morbihan', which gives 47.50, -2.87 and places the action likely near Quiberon Bay; the pool's earlier 47.55, -3.12 lies about 20 km northwest. Month and day approximate, 07-01.
stops.campa: The Veneti hold the Atlantic coast of Armorica and its harbours, and they detain the Roman officers sent to requisition grain. Their ships are oak, high-sided, flat-bottomed, rigged with leather sails, and a Roman ram does nothing to them. Decimus Brutus fits hooked poles to the galleys, runs alongside, and cuts the halyards, so the yards come down and the great hulls lie becalmed and are boarded one at a time while both armies watch from the shore. Caesar puts the entire Venetic council to death and sells the rest of the people.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Battle of Morbihan' (fetched): Decimus Junius Brutus Albinus in command, hooks on wooden poles used to cut the halyards
suggested_refs: The oak-built leather-sailed ships of the Veneti, described in Caesar's book 3

stops.name: The Rhine: a bridge in ten days, and taken down again
stops.date_confidence: The bridge and the ten-day construction are attested from Caesar's own book 4. The crossing point is disputed among modern topographers and is not resolved by any source fetched; the coordinate is an approximate regional placement in the lower-middle Rhine zone. Month and day approximate, 06-01.
stops.campa: The Usipetes and Tencteri have crossed the river and Caesar destroys them. Then he decides the Germans should learn that a Roman army can come to them. The Ubii offer boats; he refuses, because a bridge is a statement and a boat is not. His engineers drive paired piles into the current at an angle, upstream and downstream, so that the force of the water tightens the structure against itself. It is finished in ten days. He crosses, burns villages, stays eighteen days, comes back, and pulls the bridge down behind him.
suggested_refs: Caesar's own description of the Rhine bridge's pile construction, book 4, and the topographers' unresolved dispute over the site

stops.name: Deal: the eagle-bearer goes over the side first
stops.date_confidence: The expedition is attested from Caesar's own book 4 and the late-August date is the conventional one. The identification of the landing beach near Deal is a long-standing but contested topographical tradition and is not confirmed by any source fetched.
stops.campa: Late in the season, with the year's fighting in Gaul finished, Caesar takes two legions across to an island about which Roman merchants can tell him almost nothing useful. The transports cannot get close enough to beach; the men will not go over the side into deep water under missiles until the eagle-bearer of the tenth legion jumps in alone and shames them after him. The cavalry transports are blown back to Gaul. A spring tide wrecks the fleet at anchor. He takes hostages, holds nothing, and sails home before the equinox. At Rome the Senate votes twenty days of public thanksgiving.
suggested_refs: The contested Deal landing site, and the alternative beaches proposed for the 55 BC crossing

stops.name: The Thames: Cassivellaunus and the four thousand chariots
stops.date_confidence: The second expedition and the Thames crossing are attested from Caesar's own book 5. The identification of the ford with the Brentford reach is a conventional modern guess and is not independently confirmed. Month and day approximate, 07-01.
stops.campa: He returns with five legions and eight hundred ships, marches inland, and forces the Thames at a ford the Britons are said to have staked below the waterline. Cassivellaunus sends his infantry home and keeps four thousand chariots, hitting the column and disappearing into woodland, a way of fighting the legions have no answer to. British tribes come over to Caesar and give up the location of the stronghold. Terms are agreed: hostages, an annual tribute, no war on the Trinovantes. The tribute is never paid once he is gone, and no Roman army comes back for ninety-seven years.
suggested_refs: The staked ford of the Thames, conventionally placed near Brentford
The Claudian invasion of AD 43, the next Roman army in Britain

stops.name: Atuatuca: fifteen cohorts lost in a wooded valley
stops.date_confidence: Attested from Caesar's own book 5. The Tongeren-area identification of Atuatuca is the standard modern placement, not independently re-verified this pass. The disaster falls in the winter of 54/53; month and day approximate, 12-01.
stops.campa: The harvest has failed and the legions are quartered further apart than usual. Ambiorix of the Eburones tells Sabinus that all Gaul is rising and offers him safe conduct out; Cotta says stay behind the rampart; they argue most of the night and Sabinus wins, and the column marches into a wooded valley in the morning. Fifteen cohorts are destroyed. Ambiorix rides to the Nervii the same day, and the camp of Quintus Cicero, brother of the orator, is under siege before Caesar knows the first camp is gone.
sources: Dossier; the Tongeren identification is standard modern scholarship
suggested_refs: The relief of Quintus Tullius Cicero's winter camp

stops.name: Avaricum: the town Vercingetorix did not want to defend
stops.date_confidence: Attested siege. Wikipedia, 'Bourges' confirms the siege, the destruction and the killing of all but 800 of the inhabitants. The population figure of roughly 40,000 is Caesar's own and is unverifiable. Month and day approximate, 03-01.
stops.campa: Vercingetorix has ordered the Bituriges to burn their own towns and starve the Romans out, and twenty go up in a day. Avaricum they beg to keep, and he lets them keep it against his own judgement. Caesar's men build a ramp eighty feet high in twenty-five days of constant rain, on short rations, and turn down his offer to lift the siege rather than watch them starve. When the wall goes they kill everyone inside, old men, women and children, in a town Caesar puts at forty thousand. Eight hundred get out to the Gallic camp. The granaries feed the Roman army for the rest of the campaign.
suggested_refs: The siege ramp of Avaricum, described in Caesar's book 7

stops.name: Alesia: eleven miles facing in, fourteen facing out
stops.date_confidence: Attested siege and surrender, September 52 BC. The Mont Auxois site above Alise-Sainte-Reine is the accepted identification. The reverse at Gergovia earlier in the same year is separately attested and has no stop of its own; it is folded into this scene. Day not fixed; 09-01 used to order the segment.
stops.campa: Beaten off the hill at Gergovia in the spring with forty-six centurions dead, Caesar corners Vercingetorix on the plateau of Alesia and builds two walls: eleven miles facing inward at the town, fourteen facing outward at the rest of Gaul, with towers, ditches flooded from the rivers, and fields of sharpened stakes in between. The Mandubii send their women and children out of the town to save the food. Caesar will not let them through the lines, and they starve in the open ground between the two walls, in view of both armies. The relief army comes, and fails. Vercingetorix rides out and puts his arms down.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Battle of Alesia' (fetched): the dual lines, the failed relief, the September 52 BC surrender
suggested_refs: The circumvallation and contravallation lines at Mont Auxois

Lionel Royer's 1899 Salon canvas 'Vercingetorix jette ses armes aux pieds de Cesar', a staging held by historians to be invented for effect; the painting belongs to Royer's own journey, see lionel_royer.journey.json

stops.name: Uxellodunum: the spring cut off, the hands cut off
stops.date_confidence: Attested from Hirtius's continuation, Bellum Gallicum book 8. Coordinate corrected to Wikipedia, 'Uxellodunum', commune of Vayrac, Lot; the pool's earlier 44.8894, 1.7889 lay 6-7 km southeast near Betaille. The Puy d'Issolud identification is the conventional archaeological placement. Month and day approximate, 07-01.
stops.campa: The last two thousand fighting men in Gaul hold a rock above the Dordogne with a spring at its foot. Caesar's engineers drive a gallery into the hillside and tap the veins feeding the spring until the water fails, and the defenders, who believe a god has turned against them, come down. Hirtius, taking up the book Caesar left unfinished, sets down the reasoning: the clemency is by now well enough known that severity will not be read as cruelty. So the hands are cut off every man who bore arms, and the men are let go alive, to be looked at.
sources: Aulus Hirtius, Bellum Gallicum book 8, as summarized in standard scholarship
suggested_refs: Puy d'Issolud, commune of Vayrac, and the archaeology of the cut spring

stops.name: Bibracte: the alphabet moved three places
stops.date_confidence: The cipher is attested; the placement is not. Suetonius, Divus Julius 56 gives no date and no place, saying only that Caesar used the method in confidential letters to Gaius Oppius and Cornelius Balbus. Caesar is attested to have wintered at Bibracte among the Aedui in 52/51, and this stop sits there purely to order the segment inside his years of military correspondence. No letter written in the cipher survives.
stops.campa: Wintering at Bibracte among the Aedui, with the fighting finished and a conquered country to be governed by post, Caesar writes to Rome. For anything that must not be read on the road, the letters to Gaius Oppius and Cornelius Balbus go out in a hand that nobody along the way can construe: the order of the alphabet displaced, D standing where A should stand, and so on through the rest. Suetonius sets out the method. Aulus Gellius says the grammarian Valerius Probus wrote a whole treatise on the hidden meaning of the letters in Caesar's correspondence, and that treatise is lost. No letter written in the cipher survives.
sources: Suetonius, Divus Julius 56 (Penelope/Loeb, fetched): '...he must substitute the fourth letter of the alphabet, namely D, for A, and so with the others'
Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights 17.9, via Wikipedia, 'Caesar cipher'
suggested_refs: Valerius Probus's lost treatise on the cipher of Caesar's letters
Augustus, Caesar's great-nephew and posthumously adopted son, who used a related shift of one without wraparound, writing Z as AA

stops.name: The Rubicon: a small river in the dark
stops.date_confidence: Attested crossing, 10 or 11 January 49 BC. The identification of the modern Fiumicino near Savignano sul Rubicone with the ancient Rubicon rests on a 1933 Italian government ruling, an administrative and scholarly identification and not an ancient-source-confirmed spot. The words spoken differ between sources and translations and are not harmonized here.
stops.campa: The Senate has voted that Caesar lay down his command by a fixed day, and the tribunes who vetoed the vote have reached his camp dressed as slaves. He spends the evening at dinner in Ravenna, then goes out and rides with a few companions in a hired carriage to the little river that bounds his province, and stops on the bank. Suetonius says he stood there a long time turning it over and spoke to those with him about the size of what one step would begin. Then he crosses in the night with a single legion and has Ariminum before morning.
stops.quote: Take we the course which the signs of the gods and the false dealing of our foes point out. The die is cast.
stops.quote_source: Suetonius, Life of Julius Caesar 32, translated J. C. Rolfe (Loeb), LacusCurtius. Plutarch, Life of Caesar 32.8 has instead the Greek imperative from Menander, 'Let the die be cast'; the Thomson and Forester translation of Suetonius reads 'We may still retreat; but if we pass this little bridge, nothing is left for us but to fight it out in arms.' The three are not reconciled.
suggested_refs: The modern Fiumicino at Savignano sul Rubicone, identified as the ancient Rubicon by Italian government ruling in 1933

stops.name: Brundisium: an empty harbour
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Pompey's evacuation from Brundisium is conventionally dated to 17 March 49 BC. The letter quoted here is Caesar's own, written in the same weeks after the surrender of Corfinium, and survives because Cicero copied it into his correspondence.
stops.campa: Italy falls to him in sixty days without a battle. At Corfinium he takes Domitius Ahenobarbus and thirty senators and lets every one of them go, keeping their money and enlisting their men; the policy is deliberate and he puts it in writing to his agents. He reaches Brundisium to find that Pompey has already crossed to Greece with the consuls, the cause of the Republic, and most of the Senate. There are no ships left in the harbour to follow with. He turns west instead, toward the Pompeian legions holding Spain.
stops.quote: Let us see if by moderation we can win all hearts and secure a lasting victory, since by cruelty others have been unable to escape from hatred and to maintain their victory for any length of time except L. Sulla, whose example I do not intend to follow. This is a new way of conquering, to strengthen one's position by kindness and generosity.
stops.quote_source: Caesar's letter to Oppius and Cornelius Balbus, spring 49 BC, quoted verbatim in Cicero, Letters to Atticus 9.7C; English translation via attalus.org. One of the very few surviving pieces of Caesar's private prose.
suggested_refs: The surrender of Corfinium and the release of Domitius Ahenobarbus

stops.name: Ilerda: a river lowered, an army surrendered
stops.date_confidence: Attested campaign from Caesar's own Bellum Civile book 1; Wikipedia, 'Lleida' confirms the stand of Afranius and Petreius with five legions and the eventual capitulation. The surrender is conventionally dated to early August 49 BC. The parallel siege of Massilia by Trebonius and Decimus Brutus runs through the same season and has no separate stop.
stops.campa: Afranius and Petreius hold Ilerda with five legions and the bridges over the Sicoris. A flood takes out Caesar's bridges and leaves his camp cut off and hungry; then he digs channels to lower the river, gets his cavalry over, and shadows the Pompeian army into waterless country until it can neither advance nor go back. The two camps begin to mix, soldiers finding brothers and cousins on the other side, until Petreius has the Caesarians inside his lines killed. Caesar sends back every one of Petreius's men who has come across to him. The army capitulates and is discharged without harm.
stops.quote: I go to meet an army without a leader, and I shall return to meet a leader without an army.
stops.quote_source: Suetonius, Life of Julius Caesar 34, translated J. C. Rolfe (Loeb), LacusCurtius. Said on setting out for Spain.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Marseille' (fetched), on the siege of Massilia in the same year
suggested_refs: The siege of Massilia, 49 BC, conducted in Caesar's absence by Trebonius and Decimus Brutus

stops.name: Dyrrachium: the lines broken, the defeat admitted
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Wikipedia, 'Durres' confirms the battle and the outcome in Pompey's favour; the breakout is conventionally dated to 10 July 48 BC. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from cicero.journey.json, which pins two of its own stops here, rather than the geography lens's 41.3133, 19.4458.
stops.campa: Caesar crosses the Adriatic in winter with half his force and is stranded for months while Bibulus's fleet holds the sea behind him. When Antony finally brings the rest over, he pins Pompey against the coast at Dyrrachium and throws fifteen miles of line around an army larger than his own, which his men hold while eating bread made out of roots. Pompey finds the seam at the southern end and breaks through it. A thousand Caesarians are lost. Caesar admits the defeat in his own dispatch, takes the army off the coast, and marches inland into Thessaly.
suggested_refs: The siege lines at Dyrrachium and the root-bread of the Caesarian legions

stops.name: Pharsalus: the fourth line
stops.date_confidence: Attested, 9 August 48 BC on the unreformed Roman calendar, per Wikipedia, 'Battle of Pharsalus', which also confirms the concealed fourth line and the rout.
stops.campa: Pompey has twice the infantry, seven times the cavalry, and a plan: the horse will roll up Caesar's right wing and take the legions from behind. Caesar pulls six cohorts out of his third line and hides them behind his own cavalry with orders to hold their javelins as spears and thrust upward at the faces of young men who care what they look like. The horse breaks and runs. The line is turned, the camp is taken with the dinner laid out on the tables inside it, and the army of the Republic is finished before noon. Pompey rides for the coast, and for Egypt.
stops.quote: They would have it so. Even I, Gaius Caesar, after so many great deeds, should have been found guilty, if I had not turned to my army for help.
stops.quote_source: Suetonius, Life of Julius Caesar 30, translated J. C. Rolfe (Loeb), LacusCurtius. Plutarch, Life of Caesar 46.1 gives a close variant, reported as spoken looking over the dead at Pharsalus.
suggested_refs: The concealed fourth line of cohorts, described in Caesar's own book 3

stops.name: Alexandria: besieged in the palace quarter
stops.date_confidence: Attested arrival and siege. Coordinate corrected to the promontory of Lochias, the northeast angle of the ancient city where the Royal Palaces stood and which Wikipedia, 'Alexandria' says has almost entirely disappeared into the sea; the pool's earlier 29.888 lay at the Pharos end of the Eastern Harbour instead. Caesar reaches Egypt in early October 48; the day is approximate.
stops.campa: Caesar reaches Alexandria four days after Pompey's murder and is handed his rival's head and signet ring, and the sources say he wept. He installs himself in the palace quarter as arbitrator between Ptolemy and his sister, which is not a thing a foreign general is invited to do, and Cleopatra has herself carried in past the guards to reach him first. Then the city rises. He is besieged in his own lodging for months, burns the fleet at its moorings to keep the harbour, and the fire takes warehouses of books along the docks. Whether it ever reached the Library itself, the evidence does not say.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Alexandria' (fetched), on the Royal Palaces at Lochias and their submersion
suggested_refs: The submerged promontory of Lochias, the modern Silsileh
The later tradition that Caesar destroyed the Library of Alexandria, which the ancient evidence does not establish for the main institution

stops.name: Alexandria: at the tomb of Alexander
stops.date_confidence: Recorded in alexander.journey.json (line 829), which lists Julius Caesar among the visitors to the Soma in antiquity along with Augustus and Caracalla. The visit is attested in the ancient tradition; no source fetched this pass gives a date, and 03-01 is used only to order the segment after the siege. Coordinate is the canonical atlas Alexandria pin, inherited byte-identical.
stops.campa: With the war in the delta over and Cleopatra on the throne, Caesar goes to the Soma, the mausoleum at the crossing of the two great streets where Alexander lies on display in his case, nearly three centuries dead and still being shown to visitors. Caesar is fifty-three. He wept in Spain at thirty-one before a statue of this man, because Alexander at that age had taken the world and he had taken nothing. He has since taken Gaul, Italy, Spain, Greece and Egypt. What he said standing at the tomb, if he said anything, no one wrote down.
sources: alexander.journey.json, line 829: the Soma at Alexandria visited in antiquity by Julius Caesar, Augustus and Caracalla
suggested_refs: The Soma of Alexander, lost since late antiquity and never located

stops.name: Zela: five days from arrival to the end
stops.date_confidence: Attested, 2 August 47 BC, per Wikipedia, 'Battle of Zela (47 BC)', which confirms the date, the forces and the scythed chariots. The context in which the three words were displayed is disputed: Suetonius says a placard in the Pontic triumph, Appian says a letter. Not resolved.
stops.campa: Pharnaces, son of Mithridates, has taken Pontus back while Rome was busy with itself, and has mutilated the Roman citizens he captured. Caesar comes up from Egypt through Syria, meets him at Zela on the same ground where Pharnaces's father once destroyed a Roman army, and is attacked uphill by scythed chariots while the legions are still digging. The whole engagement takes four hours. Five days from his arrival in the country to the end of the war. Afterwards he remarks that Pompey was lucky to have made his reputation against opponents of this quality.
stops.quote: I came, I saw, I conquered
stops.quote_source: Suetonius, Life of Julius Caesar 37, translated J. C. Rolfe (Loeb), LacusCurtius, reporting the inscription carried in Caesar's Pontic triumph. Appian instead places the phrase in a letter.
suggested_refs: The placard of the Pontic triumph, and Appian's competing account of a letter

stops.name: Thapsus: the elephants turned back into the line
stops.date_confidence: Attested, 6 April 46 BC on the unreformed calendar, per Wikipedia, 'Battle of Thapsus', which confirms the forces, the elephant corps and the archers. The killing after the line broke is reported by the anonymous author of the Bellum Africum, who was there.
stops.campa: In Africa the remnant of the Senate's cause has Juba's Numidian cavalry, sixty war elephants, and Metellus Scipio, who holds that a Scipio commanding in Africa is halfway to a prophecy. Caesar traps the army against the sea at Thapsus. His archers shoot at the elephants' faces until the animals turn and go back through their own line. Then the legions kill past the point where orders reach them: the officer who writes the campaign up says the men would not stop, and cut down Caesar's own senators as they tried to surrender. At Utica, Cato opens his belly rather than be pardoned.
suggested_refs: Cato's suicide at Utica and Caesar's Anticato

stops.name: Rome, the Temple of Venus Genetrix: the goddess in the family
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Wikipedia, 'Temple of Venus Genetrix': dedicated to the goddess on 26 September 46 BC by Julius Caesar, on the last day of the quadruple triumph. Cicero's Pro Marcello was delivered to the Senate in the same year, though not on this day.
stops.campa: On the last day of four triumphs, Gallic, Egyptian, Pontic and African, Caesar dedicates the temple of Venus Genetrix at the head of the new forum he has built alongside the Senate house. The goddess is the mother of Aeneas, Aeneas the father of Iulus, Iulus the founder of the Julian line: the descent Caesar claimed aloud at twenty-nine, standing over his aunt's coffin, is now masonry, and paid for out of Gaul. Inside, beside the goddess, stands a gilded statue of Cleopatra. In the Senate that same year Cicero stands up and thanks him publicly for sparing one man's life.
stops.quote: such great humanity, such unprecedented and unheard-of clemency, such moderation in the exercise of supreme and universal power, such incredible and almost godlike wisdom
stops.quote_source: Cicero, Pro Marcello, delivered before the Senate in 46 BC with Caesar present; Perseus Digital Library
suggested_refs: The Forum Iulium and its surviving travertine and tufa foundations, documented from the sixteenth century by Palladio and Labacco

stops.name: Rome: the year of four hundred and forty-five days
stops.date_confidence: Attested reform. Pliny names Sosigenes among the astronomers who advised. The intercalation belongs to 46 BC and the reformed calendar takes effect on 1 January 45 BC; the stop is dated to the last day of the long year, which is a device for ordering the segment rather than a recorded event.
stops.campa: The Roman year has drifted so far from the sun that the harvest festivals are being kept in spring. As pontifex maximus, Caesar takes the calendar in hand with Sosigenes and other astronomers and fixes the year at three hundred and sixty-five days with one day added every fourth year. To bring the seasons back into line first, he inserts two extra months into this single year, so that 46 runs to four hundred and forty-five days, the longest year anyone has lived through. People complain about it bitterly. The new calendar takes effect on the first day of the following January.
sources: Pliny, Natural History, naming Sosigenes among Caesar's advisers (reported in dossier)
suggested_refs: The annus confusionis of 46 BC and the Julian calendar in force from 1 January 45 BC

stops.name: Munda: eight hours, and a line that does not move
stops.date_confidence: Attested, 17 March 45 BC. Wikipedia, 'Battle of Munda' confirms the eight-hour engagement and the fight-for-his-life remark, and corrects the pool: Gnaeus Pompeius was not captured and killed at Munda but escaped the field and was cornered and killed weeks later at the Battle of Lauro. Labienus and Attius Varus died on the field and were given burial by Caesar's order. Sextus remained at large.
stops.campa: Pompey's sons have raised thirteen legions in Spain, and Titus Labienus, who was Caesar's best officer for nine years in Gaul and went over to the other side at the Rubicon, commands their cavalry. The armies meet on a slope near Munda and for eight hours the line does not move. Caesar goes into the front rank bareheaded, and says afterwards that he had often fought for victory but that day he fought for his life. Thirty thousand die. Labienus is killed on the field and buried on Caesar's order. Gnaeus Pompey gets away, is cornered at Lauro weeks later, and is killed there.
suggested_refs: The Battle of Lauro, where Gnaeus Pompeius was killed weeks after Munda

stops.name: Rome, the Forum: the diadem refused at the Lupercalia
stops.date_confidence: Attested date of the Lupercalia and multiply attested episode: Suetonius, Plutarch, Cassius Dio and Nicolaus of Damascus. The dictatorship in perpetuity, voted earlier in the same year, is folded into this scene. No reliable evidence establishes that Caesar had a settled plan to take the title of king; the conspirators' fear that he did is a separate fact from the intention.
stops.campa: Caesar has been made dictator in perpetuity. His image is carried in procession among those of the gods, his statue stands among the kings, a month of the year now has his name on it. At the Lupercalia, with the naked runners going round the Palatine and striking women with strips of hide, Antony comes up to the platform and holds out a diadem wound with laurel. A few people applaud. Caesar pushes it away and the whole Forum roars, and he orders it carried to the Capitol, since Jupiter alone is king at Rome. The refusal is entered in the public records.
sources: Multiply attested ancient tradition: Suetonius, Plutarch, Cassius Dio, Nicolaus of Damascus
suggested_refs: The entry in the fasti recording the diadem offered and refused

stops.name: Rome, the Curia of Pompey: twenty-three wounds
stops.date_confidence: Attested, the Ides of March 44 BC, in the Curia of Pompey within the Theatre of Pompey complex, Caesar's own Curia being unfinished. Suetonius reports the physician Antistius finding twenty-three wounds, of which one, the second, to the chest, was judged mortal. Canonical Rome pin, inherited byte-identical from cicero.journey.json, whose own stop places Cicero in the chamber that morning.
stops.campa: The Senate meets in the hall attached to Pompey's theatre, because Caesar's own is not finished. He has dismissed the Spanish bodyguard. Tillius Cimber comes forward with a petition about his exiled brother and takes hold of the toga at both shoulders; Casca strikes at the neck from behind and makes a poor job of it. Then they are all on him, sixty men in a space too small for sixty men, wounding each other in the press, and he goes down at the base of Pompey's statue and pulls the toga over his head. Antistius the physician counts twenty-three wounds and judges one of them mortal.
stops.quote: What! art thou, too, one of them! Thou, my son!
stops.quote_source: Suetonius, Life of Julius Caesar 82, translated Thomson and Forester, read verbatim at Perseus. Suetonius gives this only as what 'some authors relate' when Marcus Brutus struck, and elsewhere says it is not known whether Caesar spoke at all, reporting that he merely groaned. This translation carries no Greek 'kai su, teknon'. 'Et tu, Brute' is Shakespeare and is not an ancient quotation.
sources: Suetonius, Divus Julius 81-82 (Penelope/Loeb, fetched; and Thomson/Forester via Perseus)
cicero.journey.json, stop 'Rome, the Curia of Pompey, the Ides of March'
suggested_refs: The Curia of Pompey at Largo di Torre Argentina, cleared from 1909 and excavated in the demolitions of 1926-1929, which in 1927 turned up the colossal head and arms of a marble statue
The no-kill cat sanctuary founded in the ruins in 1993; public walkways were announced in 2019 and opened in June 2023

stops.name: Rome, the Forum: the pyre, and the comet
stops.date_confidence: The funeral is attested but not precisely dated; 20 March is the conventional placement. The comet appears in July 44 BC during Octavian's games and is folded into this stop rather than given its own. Coordinate is the site of the pyre and of the later Temple of Divus Iulius, dedicated by Augustus on 18 August 29 BC; the afterlife lens's 41.89253, 12.48611 is superseded by the article's own 41.8919, 12.4862, which the geography lens also gave.
stops.campa: The body lies in the house until the funeral. In the Forum, Antony reads the will, which leaves the gardens across the Tiber to the people and three hundred sesterces to every man in the city, and holds up the pierced toga where they can see it. The crowd will not let the pyre wait for the Campus Martius and burns him where he lies, feeding the fire with benches, with the musicians' costumes, with their own clothes. They raise a column on the spot and the consuls have it taken down. In July a comet burns seven nights over the games his heir is holding in his name, and Rome decides it is his soul going up.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Temple of Caesar' (fetched), citing Suetonius and Cassius Dio; Suetonius 84-85 could not be fetched directly, the page truncating before that point
Suetonius, Divus Julius (Penelope/Loeb) on the comet interpreted as Caesar's spirit ascending
suggested_refs: The Temple of Divus Iulius, built by Augustus on the cremation site and dedicated 18 August 29 BC; only the concrete platform core survives, the marble stripped in the late fifteenth century
The round altar in the temple platform marking the spot of the pyre, where flowers are still left, in greater number each 15 March
